# University of Edinburgh: Concise Summary
The University of Edinburgh, founded in 1582 by royal charter, is one of Scotland's most historic and prestigious institutions. Its Central Area forms the original campus and is complemented by King's Buildings (Science and Engineering), BioQuarter (medicine), Easter Bush (veterinary medicine), and Western General (genetics/cancer research), housing modern and historic buildings like Old College, McEwan Hall, and Teviot Row House—the world’s oldest purpose-built students’ union. It is governed by the University Court, General Council, and Senatus Academicus, and led by Principal Sir Peter Mathieson, Chancellor Princess Anne, and current Rector Simon Fanshawe. In 2002, it reorganised into three colleges: Arts, Humanities and Social Sciences; Medicine and Veterinary Medicine; and Science & Engineering, with a total of 21 schools.
Academically, Edinburgh is recognised internationally—ranking 4th in UK research power (2021 REF), routinely placing in the global top 30, and holding membership in the Russell Group, Coimbra Group, and several other major alliances. It has produced numerous breakthroughs, including electromagnetic theory (James Clerk Maxwell), antiseptic surgery (Joseph Lister), economics (Adam Smith), geology (James Hutton), and the cloning of Dolly the sheep. With an endowment of over £580 million and more than 12,600 staff, the university attracts a highly diverse student body: in 2024, 66,293 applications resulted in 7,302 enrolments, with substantial international representation and a strong commitment to widening access. Student life is vibrant, featuring over 250 societies, the world’s oldest varsity rugby match, and strong traditions in media, music, and theatre. Alumni include 20 Nobel laureates and many heads of state.
